pages.name: The arc goes out at a peak
pages.text: The arc struck once at L1's peak and went out almost at once, at a current zero. The dashed line shows the star point held 359 V from the hull.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. No losses. One strike: the arc went out at a peak and left the star point held away from the hull, so L1 swings about it.

pages.name: Once the arc is out
pages.task: The arc has just gone out at a current zero. What does the star point's voltage to the hull do now?
pages.answer: It stays 359 V from the hull, held by the charge on the capacitance
pages.why: The arc went out as the capacitance reached its peak. The charge has no quick way off, only slow leakage. So the star point stays 359 V from the hull. L1 swings about it.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. No losses. One strike: the arc went out at a peak and left the star point held away from the hull, so L1 swings about it.
options: It falls back to 0 V, as the fault has gone
It stays 359 V from the hull, held by the charge on the capacitance
It swings at 60 Hz about the hull, as before the fault

pages.name: The gap restrikes
pages.text: With no losses, the second strike lands when L1 is 718 V from the hull. The star point rings past and is held at 1,077 V.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. No losses. 2 strikes: each restrike leaves the star point further out, and L1's peaks climb.

pages.name: The next peak
pages.task: There are no losses. After the second strike, the star point is held at 1,077 V. That is three times the normal peak of 359 V. How high does L1 peak half a cycle later?
pages.answer: 1,436 V, the held voltage plus L1's own swing
pages.why: L1's far peak is 1,077 + 359 = 1,436 V, 4 times normal. With no losses, the climb goes on until a weak part fails. A starter coil or a motor winding often goes first.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. No losses. 3 strikes: each restrike leaves the star point further out, and L1's peaks climb.
options: 1,077 V, the voltage the star point holds
1,436 V, the held voltage plus L1's own swing
718 V, twice the normal peak

pages.name: Losses damp the ring
pages.text: With Some losses and three strikes, L1 peaks at 718 V, 1,077 V, then 1,257 V. The climb is levelling off.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. Some losses. 3 strikes: each restrike leaves the star point a little further out, and L1's peaks climb, then level off.

pages.name: Heavy losses
pages.task: Heavy losses damp the ring completely. The star point never rings past. The arc restrikes at every peak. How high does L1 get?
pages.answer: 718 V, twice its normal peak, and no higher
pages.why: The first strike holds the star point 359 V out, so L1 reaches 718 V. Each restrike only flips it to 359 V on the other side. 718 V is a little above the 622 V peak that a solid fault puts on the healthy lines.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. Heavy losses. 3 strikes: each restrike only flips the star point to the other side, and L1's peaks stay the same.
options: 359 V, its normal peak, as the losses stop any rise
718 V, twice its normal peak, and no higher
It still climbs, only more slowly

pages.name: Filters on an insulated supply
pages.text: With the filters in, a solid first fault passes 575 mA. The monitor settles twice as slowly. With them out, the fault passes 287 mA, and the EMC tag is red.

pages.name: A reading that jumps
pages.task: A new drive's filter is out, as it should be on an insulated supply. Yet the monitor's reading jumps about whenever the drive runs. What do you check first?
pages.answer: That the monitor is made for supplies that feed drives
pages.why: A drive's rectifier joins its DC side to the supply. DC leaking from there distorts a plain monitor's reading. So use a monitor made for non-linear loads.

pages.name: Touching a floating supply
pages.text: With a solid fault on L1, a person on the hull touching L2 holds 440 V. About 440 mA flows through a 1,000 Ω body.

pages.name: A healthy reading
pages.task: The monitor reads 2 MΩ, with no alarm. The cables have 1 µF a line. You stand on the hull and touch L1. What flows through a 1,000 Ω body?
pages.answer: About 190 mA, back through the cables' capacitance
pages.why: The monitor reads resistance with DC or a very slow AC, so the capacitance barely shows. But the capacitance passes AC and closes the loop through you. About 190 mA flows. A healthy reading is no reason to touch.

pages.name: Two sides of the argument
pages.task: One side says an arcing fault can pump an insulated supply's voltage up. The other says this is not a problem on ships. What does each case rest on?
pages.answer: The first on voltages measured on 480 V systems, the second on ships' heavier losses
pages.why: Engineers measured 1,200 V or more on 480 V systems.[^1] The marine case is that ships' heavy losses damp the ring. With light losses the ladder climbs. Heavy losses stop it. People still argue where a real ship sits.
pages.alt: A sketch of L1 on a 440 V, 60 Hz insulated supply, with the system capacitance and an arc gap at a chafed cable, both to the hull. Below, a plot of L1's voltage to the hull against time, slowed down, with the star point's voltage dashed. Heavy losses. 3 strikes: each restrike only flips the star point to the other side, and L1's peaks stay the same.
options: The first on voltages measured on 480 V systems, the second on ships' heavier losses
The first on theory alone, the second on measurements at sea
Both on the same measurements, read differently

pages.name: What the filter gave
pages.task: You disconnect a drive's EMC filter so it suits an insulated supply. What have you given up?
pages.answer: Its full EMC performance, so more switching noise can reach nearby equipment
pages.why: Without the filter, the drive may no longer meet its EMC standard. In return, the supply stays floating, with less capacitance to the hull.
